1.goal: To open the lesson through the operation it teaches: two texts about the same night that stop agreeing somewhere, and someone who needs to be told what the difference changes.
1.interaction: T–S, one open question. Portuguese is accepted here; the idea matters more than the language.
run: Read the question on screen with him and take one answer.
A real case or an invented one both work — what you want is the situation, not the story. Keep it to one example.
1.expected: Something from his own work: two witness statements that do not match · a client's version against a police report · a file that changed between one hearing and the next.
1.support: If he describes reading ONE document, bring him back to the pair: the work today is the comparison, not the reading. If he answers in Portuguese, take the idea and say it back in English for him to repeat — do not stop the idea to fix the language.
1.challenge: Ask what he did with the difference once he found it: who he told, and what that person did next.
1.monitoring: Whether he says what the difference CHANGED for the person listening. That is the lesson in one sentence.
1.evidence: The example he gives, and what the difference changed. Worth writing down for the post-lesson record.
1.transition: Move on when he has given one concrete example.

2.goal: To establish who is asking, what she is asking for, and what she will do with the answer — so that everything he reads afterwards has a destination.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the message on screen together.
run: Give him time to read the message.
Then confirm two things out loud: Claire has read neither text, and she has to repeat what he tells her to a third person.
Take the question on screen in one sentence.
Where the two texts diverge is deliberately NOT said here. That arrives with his own first reading, at stage 3.
exact: What does Claire need from you, and what will she do with it?
2.expected: Where the two texts stop agreeing, and which part is in the documents and which part is his own reading — because she has to pass it on and cannot check it herself.
2.support: If the message reads as background, ask what happens to Claire's note if he gets the second half wrong.
2.challenge: Ask what he would want to know about the third person before deciding how much detail to give.
2.monitoring: Whether he notices the second half of the request — the separation between what the documents say and what he concluded. It is the criterion the whole lesson is built on.
2.evidence: Whether the separation appears in his own words here, before it is taught. It is the baseline for stage 6.
2.transition: Move on when he has said, in one sentence, what Claire needs from him.

3.goal: To activate what he already knows about why two honest versions differ, BEFORE he sees either text. He argues this for a living in Portuguese; the point is to have it in English first.
3.interaction: T–S, three open questions. Hypotheses, not answers.
run: Read the three questions with him, out loud, and ask for a guess on each.
Do not correct and do not confirm: these are predictions, and the texts check them at stage 4.
exact: If a guess comes in one word: “Why that one?”
3.expected: The report is likely to be exact about the hour, because it is written to a form, with a clock · the witness is likely to know who spoke first, because she was in the exchange · no — two accounts can differ without either being false. Any of the three may come out the other way round; what matters is the reason he gives.
3.support: If he answers with one word, ask “why that one?” once. The reason is the part that transfers to the briefing.
3.challenge: Ask which of the three he would still defend after reading both texts, and to say now what would change his mind.
3.monitoring: This is one of the few moments where his long turns cost nothing. Let him talk.
3.evidence: The reasons he gives — they come back as the argument of the briefing at stage 8.
3.transition: Move on when he has risked an answer on all three.

4.goal: To read each text for what IT is — who wrote it, for what, and what it does not set out to say — before any comparison.
4.interaction: S reads alone, in silence, then T–S one text at a time.
run: Both texts are on this screen. Two minutes each, in silence, one after the other — the account first, then the report.
Then ask, for each one in turn: who wrote this, why, and what is it not trying to say?
Do not let the two questions merge into one comparison.
exact: Who wrote this, for what, and what does it not set out to say?
If he starts comparing: “Hold that for two minutes.”
4.expected: The account is one person's version, written by someone who was in the exchange; it can say what she saw and felt, and it does not set out to describe what happened afterwards · the report is a record made to a form by someone who arrived later; it registers what was found and what was stated at the time, and it does not set out to say what anyone meant.
4.support: He will want to compare immediately — it is his professional reflex, and it is a strength. Hold him here anyway: comparing before understanding each piece produces a list of differences with no judgment of which ones matter.
4.challenge: Ask which of the two he would rather have if he could only take one into the hearing, and why.
4.monitoring: This is the first isolated reading sample of the cycle. Note how he reads: what he goes back to, what he skips, and whether he reads the source line at all.
4.evidence: How he reads under no time pressure — the reading sample the cycle is measured against.
4.transition: Move on when he has said, in one sentence each, what the two texts are.

5.goal: To attribute each statement to its source, including the two that belong to neither text alone.
5.interaction: S works alone on the six, then T–S on the two limit cases.
run: He does the six on his own first.
The two texts are on this screen, under “Show the two texts” — this is attribution, not memory, so let him open them and point at the line.
Only when he has finished all six does he press Check; the explanation opens with it.
exact: “Nobody is recorded as leaving” — which of the two says that? (Both.)
“She was frightened” — where is that written? (Nowhere.)
5.expected: 1 the witness account (four people) · 2 the incident report (23:40) · 3 both of them (nobody recorded as leaving) · 4 neither of them (she was frightened) · 5 the incident report (she addressed the group) · 6 the witness account (someone in the group spoke first).
5.support: If he is stuck on one, send him back to the text to find the line rather than answering it — the operation being practiced is finding it.
5.challenge: Ask him to say, for item 4, what he would have to ask Ms. Ferraz for it to become supported.
5.monitoring: Items 3 and 4. The agreement matters as much as the divergences: a briefing that lists only disagreement sounds like an accusation. And item 4 is the one he will be tempted to say out loud at stage 8.
5.evidence: Whether he opens the texts or answers from memory, and which of the two limit cases he gets without help.
5.transition: Move on when he has the two limit cases right, with or without a first attempt.

6.goal: To separate what a text STATES from what the reader CONCLUDED — and from what he would ask for. He makes this distinction in Portuguese with precision; the work here is the English that marks it.
6.interaction: S classifies alone, then T–S on the question that carries the lesson.
run: He classifies the six on his own, with the texts available under “Show the two texts”.
Then Check: each wrong line shows what it was, and the explanation opens.
Then ask the question below, which is the one that carries the lesson.
exact: Which of these would you say in a hearing without marking where it came from?
“Somebody left before the officer arrived” — does either text say that? (No.) Is it false, then? (Unknown — it is a conclusion, and a conclusion gets marked as one.)
6.expected: 1 it is in the text · 2 I concluded it (somebody left) · 3 it is in the text · 4 it is what I would ask for (why the group was there) · 5 I concluded it (she was not the one who started it) · 6 it is in the text.
6.support: If he explains the concept in Portuguese, agree with the content and ask for it in English. The concept is not what is missing.
6.challenge: Ask him to turn one line of the middle column into something he could say in a hearing, and to name what he had to add.
6.monitoring: The middle column. Nothing in it is wrong to say — it is wrong to say it in the sentence that belongs to the first column.
6.evidence: Whether he names the middle column as the one to mark when he speaks. That is what stage 8 measures under load.
6.transition: Move on when he names the middle column as the one that has to be marked when he speaks.

7.goal: To produce the attribution out loud, with support on screen, before producing it without.
7.interaction: T points at a statement; S says the full sentence. Six of them, at speed.
run: The six statements are on this screen, on the left; the openings are on the right.
You point at one statement, he says the full sentence with the source built into it. You give the content, he gives the sentence.
Pronunciation: “according to” runs as one word, stressed on CORD. “States” is one syllable.
Seven minutes, and the next stage is the longest of the lesson. If he starts explaining the case, cut in gently.
exact: If he starts explaining the case: “That is the briefing — hold it for two minutes.”
7.expected: According to the account, there were four of them on the corner · The report states that three individuals were present · Both of them say that nobody is recorded as leaving · Neither of them mentions that she was frightened · The report says she addressed the group; she claims the opposite · As far as I can tell, the difference that matters is who spoke first.
7.support: If the source keeps arriving after the claim, stop that one sentence and ask for it again from the opening.
7.challenge: Point at two statements at once and ask for both in a single sentence, with the sources kept apart.
7.monitoring: Whether he still needs the openings on screen by the fifth and sixth.
7.evidence: On how many of the six the source arrives inside the sentence without support. It is the number to compare with the briefing.
7.transition: Move on when he attaches the source without looking at the openings on the last two.

8.goal: The product of the lesson — the briefing, with the texts out of sight.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are Claire; the turn is his.
run: Close the texts on the screen before he starts.
Interrupt ONCE, in the middle, with the question below, and let him find his way back on his own.
Around three minutes is the size of the task; do not announce the time and do not stop him on it.
After you ask, WAIT. The lesson-8 analysis recorded the teacher at 63% of speaking time against 37% for the student, where the level asks for 30–50%. His silence is work, not a gap to fill.
Do not correct during. Note it and hand it back at stage 9 — correcting mid-briefing turns a production into a dialogue, which is the one thing this stage cannot become.
exact: So which one do I put in my note?
8.expected: Both texts placed in one sentence each, the divergences attributed, the agreement named, and a close on what still has to be decided.
8.support: If he stops after the interruption, repeat his last claim back to him as a question and wait. Do not restart the briefing for him.
8.challenge: Ask a second question of substance at the end — “and if the note has to fit two lines?” — and take the shorter version.
8.monitoring: Whether the source stays attached now that the text is off screen · whether he names the agreement and not only the divergences · whether “she was frightened” comes out as if it were in the account · whether he closes on what neither text says.
8.evidence: One sentence of the briefing, written down as he said it. It is the third field of the next screen.
8.transition: Move on when he closes by saying what still has to be decided.

9.goal: To give back what you noted during the briefing, and to ask for it again under a different condition.
9.interaction: T–S, filling the four fields together, then one retask.
run: Fill the four fields on screen WITH him, not about him: what worked, one point to build on, one sentence as he said it, and the same sentence made clearer.
Two points at most — a third stops being feedback and becomes a lesson.
Then open the retask. No new content here: it is the same task under one changed condition.
exact: Same briefing. Claire has now read the report, but not the account.
9.expected: He drops the explanation of the report — she has read it — and opens on where the account differs from what she already knows.
9.support: If the second version comes out the same as the first, ask what Claire already knows and what she does not.
9.challenge: Ask for the same briefing in two sentences, keeping both sources.
9.monitoring: What he CUTS when the same content has to fit a shorter turn. If the source attribution is what goes, it is not automatic yet.
9.evidence: What survived the cut. It goes in the post-lesson record, and it is what tells you whether the attribution is automatic.
9.transition: Move on when the retask has been given once, whole.

10.goal: To name what the lesson worked on, and to leave the next one already announced.
10.interaction: T–S over the list; the confidence row is his alone.
run: Read the list on screen with him and ask which of the six he would use tomorrow without preparing it. One answer is enough.
The confidence row is his — do not argue with it.

Homework, said out loud and never put on screen: the post-class has two optional recordings and two TED talks on why two honest witnesses diverge. Tell him the second one, by a forensic expert, is this lesson done at full length by someone who does it for a living.
Announce lesson 10: listening — a talk at real speed, no transcript, and a question formed on the spot. He will recognize the scene from his own conferences.
10.expected: One phrase named as usable tomorrow, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If nothing is named, read the six back to him and ask which one he would have wanted in the last briefing he actually gave.
10.challenge: Ask when the next briefing like this one is, and which of the six he will take into it.
10.monitoring: A low mark on attribution after a briefing that held it is worth recording: it is the gap between doing and knowing that he did.
10.evidence: Fill in the post-lesson record before you close. This is lesson 9 of the block, and the lesson that closes it at 12 reads the four together.
